claim: The multFYLM consists of six closely spaced, independent microfluidic subsystems, with a total capacity of 2352 cells.
source: The multFYLM consists of six closely spaced, independent microfluidic subsystems, with a total capacity of 2352 cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which show the device structure.

claim: Each subsystem of the multFYLM consists of eight parallel rows of 49 cell catch channels.
source: Each subsystem consists of eight parallel rows of 49 cell catch channels (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D showing the subsystem structure.

claim: More than 80% of the 224 monitored catch channels in each of the six microfluidic sub-systems were routinely filled.
source: we routinely filled >80% of the 224 monitored catch channels in each of the six microfluidic sub-systems (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing loading efficiency data.

claim: Up to 98% of the cells could be retained in their respective catch channels for over 100 hr.

evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C and Video 1 showing retention efficiency data.

claim: Cells within the multFYLM grew with kinetics and morphology similar to cells in liquid culture.
source: Cells within the multFYLM grew with kinetics and morphology similar to cells in liquid culture and showed growth and NETO rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A) similar to those reported previously (Coelho et al., 2013; Nobs and Maerkl, 2014; Forsburg and Rhind, 2006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A, and citations to previous studies.

claim: The fission yeast survival curve did not fit the traditional aging-dependent Gompertz model.
source: Surprisingly, the fission yeast survival curve did not fit the traditional aging-dependent Gompertz model, (Gompertz, 1825; Greenwood, 1928; Wilson, 1993), which describes survival and hazard in terms of a generation-dependent (i.e., aging) and a generation-independent term (Equation (2) in Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to the Gompertz model literature and reference to the mathematical equation.

claim: The RLS data for fission yeast were best described by a single exponential decay.
source: The RLS data were best described by a single exponential decay, corresponding to a generation-independent hazard rate.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the mathematical analysis of the survival data.

claim: The hazard rate for fission yeast remains steady at an average ~2% chance of death per cell per generation.
source: Strikingly, the hazard rate does not increase as the replicative age increases; instead, it remains steady at an average ~2% chance of death per cell per generation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by the hazard function analysis.

claim: The budding yeast hazard function increases with each generation and fits the aging-dependent Gompertz model.
source: As expected, the budding yeast hazard function increases with each generation and fits the aging-dependent Gompertz model.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by analysis of budding yeast survival data.

claim: The replicative lifespan (RLS) of strain h- 972 grown in rich media is 39.2 generations (95% C.I. 38.6–39.8, n = 440).

claim: Strain CBS2777 had the shortest RLS of 22.7 generations (95% CI 21.9–23.6 generations).

claim: Strains NCYC132 and JB760 showed greater longevity with estimated RLS of >50 and >70 generations, respectively.
